title: Data Systems
text:
What is a Data System?
A data system is a collection of interconnected components used to collect, store, process, and analyze data.

Input: Raw data (logs, transactions, sensor readings).
Process: Transformation and cleaning.
Storage: Databases or Data Lakes.
Output: Insights, reports, or machine learning models.


Think of a data system like a water treatment plant. You have raw water (input), a filtration system (processing), a reservoir (storage), and tap water for consumption (output).

title: Data Systems
text:
Data Types: The Big Picture
Data is categorized based on how much “organization” it has before it enters a system.

Structured: Highly organized (e.g., Excel, SQL).
Semi-structured: Organized but flexible (e.g., JSON, XML).
Unstructured: No predefined model (e.g., Video, PDF, Audio).


Understanding the format of your data determines what kind of database you need and how much work you have to do to clean it.

title: Data Systems
text:
Structured Data

Tabular (rows and columns).
Highly organized.
Easily searchable.
Examples:

Customer names and addresses.
Transaction amounts and dates.
Inventory counts.



Structured data is the most common form of data handled by traditional businesses. It fits perfectly into spreadsheets and relational databases.

title: Data Systems
text:
Semi-Structured Data

Does not reside in a rigid grid.
Contains tags or markers to separate data elements.
Flexible schema (can change easily).
Examples:

JSON: Used in web APIs.
XML: Used in configuration files.
CSV: Simple comma-separated values.



Semi-structured data is the “middle ground.” It has some hierarchy and markers, but you can add new fields without rebuilding the whole table.

title: Data Systems
text:
Unstructured Data

No internal structure or predefined model.
Makes up the vast majority of data generated today.
Requires specialized tools (AI/ML) to extract meaning.
Examples:

Emails (the text part).
Images and Videos.
Social media posts.



Think of a photo. A computer just sees a bunch of pixels. It doesn’t know it’s a “cat” until an unstructured data processing tool (like an AI model) analyzes it.

title: Data Systems
text:
Visualizing Data Hierarchy





%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'primaryColor': '#811331', 'edgeLabelBackground':'#ffffff', 'primaryTextColor': '#ffffff', 'lineColor': '#000000' }}}%%
graph TD
    A[Data Types] --> B[Structured]
    A --> C[Semi-Structured]
    A --> D[Unstructured]
    B --> B1[Tables/SQL]
    C --> C1[JSON/XML]
    D --> D1[Media/Text]







This diagram shows the hierarchy. As you move from top to bottom, the level of inherent organization decreases.

title: Data Systems
text:
Activity 1: Identify the Type
Identify whether the following are Structured, Semi-Structured, or Unstructured:

A .mp4 video file from a security camera.
A .json file containing a user’s profile settings.
A SQL table containing 1,000,000 rows of sales transactions.
A collection of scanned handwritten notes.
An XML file used for configuration.


Take 2 minutes to think about these. (Answers: 1. Unstructured, 2. Semi-structured, 3. Structured, 4. Unstructured, 5. Semi-structured).

title: Data Systems
text:
Relational Databases (RDBMS)
The traditional way of storing structured data.

Core Concept: Data is organized into tables.
Schema: Rigid and predefined (must define columns before inserting data).
Relationships: Tables are linked via “Keys” (Primary and Foreign keys).
Example: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle.


In a relational database, if you want to add a “Phone Number” column, you have to update the entire table structure first. This is called a “schema change.”

title: Data Systems
text:
Relational Properties: ACID
To ensure data integrity, RDBMS follow ACID properties:

Atomicity: “All or nothing” transactions.
Consistency: Data follows all rules (no broken links).
Isolation: Transactions don’t interfere with each other.
Durability: Once saved, it stays saved (even if power fails).


ACID is critical for banking. If you transfer $10, the money must leave your account AND arrive in the other account. It cannot do one without the other.

title: Data Systems
text:
Non-Relational Databases (NoSQL)
Designed for modern, high-scale, and flexible data.

Core Concept: Data is stored as documents, key-value pairs, or graphs.
Schema: Dynamic/Flexible (no predefined structure required).
Scalability: Designed to scale “out” (adding more servers).
Example: MongoDB (Document), Redis (Key-Value), Neo4j (Graph).


NoSQL is the response to the “Big Data” explosion. When you have massive amounts of unstructured or semi-structured data, relational databases can struggle to scale.

title: Data Systems
text:
NoSQL Types



Type
Best For
Example




Document
Semi-structured data
MongoDB


Key-Value
Fast caching/Session data
Redis


Graph
Complex relationships
Neo4j


Column-Family
Massive scale/Analytical
Cassandra




Different NoSQL types are specialized for different tasks. A graph database is perfect for a social network where you need to track “friend of a friend” connections.

title: Data Systems
text:
Relational vs. Non-Relational



Feature
Relational (SQL)
Non-Relational (NoSQL)




Schema
Rigid / Predefined
Flexible / Dynamic


Structure
Tables (Rows/Cols)
Documents/Graphs/Key-Value


Scaling
Vertical (Bigger Server)
Horizontal (More Servers)


Data Integrity
Very High (ACID)
Varies (BASE)




If your data structure is predictable and consistency is paramount (like finance), go SQL. If your data is changing fast and you need massive scale, go NoSQL.

title: Data Systems
text:
Choosing Your Database





%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'primaryColor': '#811331', 'edgeLabelBackground':'#ffffff', 'primaryTextColor': '#ffffff', 'lineColor': '#000000' }}}%%
graph TD
    Start[Start Decision] --> Schema{Fixed Schema?}
    Schema -- Yes --> Relational[Relational / SQL]
    Schema -- No --> Scale{Need massive scale?}
    Scale -- Yes --> NoSQL[Non-Relational / NoSQL]
    Scale -- No --> Semi[Semi-Structured / Document]







A decision tree: If Schema is fixed \(\rightarrow\) Relational. If Schema is NOT fixed \(\rightarrow\) Check scale. If massive scale \(\rightarrow\) NoSQL. If not massive scale \(\rightarrow\) Document store.

title: Data Systems
text:
Activity 2: The Architect’s Dilemma
Scenario: You are building a new social media app like Instagram.
Requirements:

You need to store user profiles (Name, Email, Password).
You need to store millions of high-resolution images.
You need to store a “Follower” graph (who follows whom).

Task: Which database type (Relational or NoSQL) would you use for each requirement? Why?

This is a real-world scenario. Most big apps use a “Hybrid” approach. For example, SQL for user accounts and a NoSQL/Graph database for the social connections.

title: Data Systems
text:
Data Pipelines
Data doesn’t just sit there; it moves.
Definition: A sequence of data processing steps where a set of data is passed through a series of transformations.
Goal: To move data from a source (where it’s created) to a destination (where it’s used).

A pipeline is like a conveyor belt in a factory. Raw materials go in one end, and finished products come out the other.

title: Data Systems
text:
ETL vs. ELT
The two main ways to move data:


ETL
(Extract, Transform, Load)

Extract from source.
Transform in a staging area (cleaning/filtering).
Load into the target database.


ELT
(Extract, Load, Transform)

Extract from source.
Load directly into the target (Data Lake).
Transform inside the target database using its own power.



ETL was the standard for decades. ELT is becoming more popular because modern cloud warehouses (like Snowflake) are incredibly powerful at processing data once it’s inside.

title: Data Systems
text:
The Data Pipeline Workflow





%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'primaryColor': '#811331', 'edgeLabelBackground':'#ffffff', 'primaryTextColor': '#ffffff', 'lineColor': '#000000' }}}%%
graph LR
    Source[Source Systems] --> Ext[Extraction]
    Ext --> Trans[Transformation]
    Trans --> Load[Loading/Storage]
    Load --> Anal[Analytics/BI]







This shows the journey from the moment a user clicks a button on a website to the moment a CEO sees a chart on their dashboard. A linear flow: Source \(\rightarrow\) Extraction \(\rightarrow\) Transformation \(\rightarrow\) Loading \(\rightarrow\) Analytics.

title: Data Systems
text:
Data Pipeline Components

Source: Where data originates (App logs, DBs, APIs).
Ingestion: The process of pulling data from the source.
Processing/Transformation: Cleaning, aggregating, or renaming fields.
Storage: The final destination (Data Warehouse or Data Lake).
Orchestration: The “brain” that schedules and monitors the steps.


Orchestration is very important. If the “Extraction” step fails, the “Transformation” step shouldn’t try to run on old or broken data.

title: Data Systems
text:
Activity 3: Pipeline Mapping
Scenario: A weather station collects temperature data every minute, sends it to a server, cleans the data (removes errors), and stores it for a yearly report.
Task:
Draw (on paper or digitally) a simple diagram of this pipeline. Label your: 1. Source 2. Extraction 3. Transformation 4. Loading 5. Destination

This helps you visualize the flow. If the sensor sends a temperature of 999 degrees (an error), that’s where your “Transformation” step fixes the data.

Educational Mislearning
The purpose of this class, and college, is for you to learn about critical thinking skills and perseverance. Using AI will only teach you how to get an answer, which may or may not be correct.

You will not develop the skills needed to problem solve a challenge. Additionally, developing grit is essential to become successful in college and life. There is no easy way out and AI is an illusion to your success in life.


To learn something, it requires hours of work! If not years!

title: Data 300
text:
Trusting AI
When using AI, you must acknowledge its limitations:

Responses provided may be incorrect
Responses may not be fair
Companies may manipulate responses and/or terms of service for their benefit
Companies may not have your best interst in mind


You should always proceed with caution utilizing these tools!

title: Data 300

Stolen Work

Additionally, all these individuals are not receiving any royalties for the work to be used in creating generative AI models.

title: Data 300
text:
Privacy Concerns
The use of generative AI raises concerns of what data is being harvested from us, possibly without informed consent or knowledge of impacts.

When you use any large language models, you do not know what information is being harvested from you.


Do you want to upload your thoughts and ideas to a company that can monetize, and possibly exploit you.


Does your Professors consent with you uploading their assignments to large language models?


Stanford provided a report highlighting the risks of our personal data use in large language models.

title: Data 300
text:
Environmental Impact
In order to run these large language models, companies need to use a large amounts of energy. This is because large servers are needed to both train and execute a model.

The LA Times reports the potential impact that running AI models in California.


Additionally, Time reports that a ChatGPT query uses ten times more energy than a Google search query, and global AI demands can consume of 1 trillion gallons of water by 2027.


There are also environmental justice questions about where these data centers are constructed.

title: Data 300
text:
Worker Exploitation
The Washington Post and Time (Article 1 and Article 2) reported that AI companies utilize “digital sweatshops” to classify data points for model training.

There is a human cost from the Global South, both financially and mentally, to develop the AI models for users in the United States and Europe.


We must be conscious consumers and demand more from these companies to provide safe working conditions and livable wages.

title: Computational Setup
text:
SQL and Relational Databases


SQL (Structured Query Language) is a language used to work with relational databases.

With SQL, we can:

Retrieve data from tables
Clean and summarize data
Manage data stored in a relational database

title: Computational Setup
text:
What is SQLite?


SQLite is a lightweight relational database management system. Unlike many database systems, SQLite does not require a separate database server. A complete database can be stored in a single file, such as:
chinook.db

This makes SQLite useful for:

Learning SQL
Small and medium-sized applications
Local data storage
Prototyping
Reproducible data projects


SQLite

title: Computational Setup
text:
Install Positron


Positron is a data science IDE built on Code OSS. We can use it as an editor for SQL files and extend it with database tools.
Download Positron


Organize database project files
Write .sql scripts
Connect to SQLite databases
Run SQL queries
View query results

text:
Install VS Code
Visual Studio Code is a general-purpose code editor that supports database workflows through extensions.
Download VS Code

Install VSCodium

VSCodium

text:
Install SQLTools
In Positron, VS Code or VS Codium, open the Extensions panel.
Search for and install:

SQLTools (mtxr.sqltools)

SQLTools provides the database connection interface. The SQLite driver allows SQLTools to connect specifically to SQLite database files.
SQLTools Documentation

title: Computational Setup
text:
Workspaces
A workspace is a project folder containing the files needed for a data-management project.
A good workflow is:

Create one folder for the course.
Create a data folder for database files.
Create a sql folder for saved SQL scripts.
Open the course folder in Positron or VS Code.
Connect SQLTools to the SQLite database file.
Save your SQL work in .sql files.

The Chinook Example Database
For examples in this course, we will use the Chinook sample database.
Chinook represents a digital media store and contains related tables for:

Chinook Database

text:
Download Chinook for SQLite
Download the SQLite version of the Chinook database from the project releases:
Chinook Releases
The SQLite database file is named similar to:
Chinook_Sqlite.sqlite
For this course, you may rename it:
chinook.db
Place it in your project’s data folder.

title: Computational Setup

Open Chinook from the Terminal
From your course project folder, run:
sqlite3 data/chinook.db
If the database opens successfully, you should see a SQLite prompt similar to:
sqlite>

title: Computational Setup
text:
Useful SQLite Commands
SQLite includes special dot commands for working with the database shell.
Try:
.tables
This displays the tables in the database.
To inspect the structure of the Customer table:
.schema Customer
To exit SQLite:
.quit

title: Computational Setup
text:
SQLite Commands






Warning


SQLite dot commands such as .tables and .schema are commands for the SQLite shell. They are not SQL statements and should not be included inside SQLTools query scripts.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Create a SQLite Connection
In VS Code or Positron:

Open the Command Palette.
Search for SQLTools: Add New Connection.
Select SQLite as the database driver.
Choose the Chinook database file in your data folder.
Give the connection a name, such as Chinook.
Test and save the connection.

You can now use SQLTools to browse tables and run SQL statements.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Create a SQL File
Inside the sql folder, create a file named:
practice.sql
Use this file to save your SQL statements.
A SQL statement usually ends with a semicolon:
SELECT *
FROM Customer;

title: Computational Setup
text:
View Data from a Table
The SELECT statement retrieves data from a database table.
SELECT *
FROM Customer;
* means to return all columns.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Select Specific Columns
Usually, we only select the columns needed for an analysis.
SELECT CustomerId,
       FirstName,
       LastName,
       Country
FROM Customer;
This makes the query output easier to read and reduces unnecessary data retrieval.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Limit Query Results
Use LIMIT when you only want to inspect a small number of rows.
SELECT CustomerId,
       FirstName,
       LastName,
       Country
FROM Customer
LIMIT 10;

title: Data Modeling
text:
Data Modeling
Data modeling is the process of describing how data is organized, connected, and constrained before building a database.

Welcome students and frame data modeling as the planning step before implementation. Emphasize that a good model reduces confusion, duplication, and future redesign.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Why Data Modeling Matters
A data model helps teams agree on:

What data must be stored
How different concepts relate
Which rules protect data quality
How the database supports real questions


Ask students to imagine building a database without a plan. Use examples like duplicate customer records, missing orders, or unclear relationships between students and courses.

title: Data Modeling
text:
From Real World to Database
Data modeling translates real-world objects and processes into database structures.





flowchart LR
  A[Real-world process] --> B[Conceptual model]
  B --> C[Logical model]
  C --> D[Physical database]

  classDef blue fill:#0072B2,color:#FFFFFF,stroke:#111111,stroke-width:2px
  classDef orange fill:#E69F00,color:#000000,stroke:#111111,stroke-width:2px
  classDef green fill:#009E73,color:#000000,stroke:#111111,stroke-width:2px
  classDef purple fill:#CC79A7,color:#000000,stroke:#111111,stroke-width:2px

  class A blue
  class B orange
  class C green
  class D purple







Explain that models become more detailed over time. Conceptual models focus on ideas, logical models focus on structure, and physical models focus on implementation details.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Three Levels of Data Models
Conceptual model:

Big-picture view
Main entities and relationships

Logical model:

Tables, fields, keys, and constraints

Physical model:

Specific DBMS details, indexes, data types, and storage choices


Use this slide to separate planning from implementation. Students often jump straight to tables, but conceptual thinking helps them understand the domain first.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Entity-Relationship Diagrams
An Entity-Relationship diagram, or ER diagram, visually represents:

Entities
Attributes
Relationships
Cardinality rules


Define ER diagrams as a communication tool. They help non-programmers and technical users discuss the structure of a database before writing SQL.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Entities
An entity is a thing about which we want to store data.
Examples:

Student
Course
Instructor
Enrollment
Product
Order


Emphasize that entities often become tables in a relational database. Ask students to name entities from a familiar system such as a library, store, or university.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Attributes
An attribute is a fact or property stored about an entity.
For a Student entity, attributes might include:

student_id
first_name
last_name
email
major


Point out that attributes often become columns. Encourage students to distinguish attributes from entities. For example, a student’s name is usually an attribute, while student is the entity.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Activity: Identify Entities and Attributes
Scenario: A college wants to track students, courses, instructors, departments, and course enrollments.
List:

At least 3 entities
At least 2 attributes per entity


Give students 8 to 10 minutes. Walk around and check whether they are mixing up entities and attributes. Bring the class back by asking for one example entity and its attributes.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Relationships
A relationship describes how entities are connected.
Examples:

A student enrolls in a course
An instructor teaches a course
A department offers many courses
An order contains products


Explain that relationships are usually verbs or actions connecting nouns. Encourage students to write relationships as short sentences.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Cardinality
Cardinality describes how many records can participate in a relationship.
Common types:

One-to-one
One-to-many
Many-to-many


Introduce cardinality as the rules of participation. Use practical wording: one student can enroll in many courses; one course can have many students.

title: Data Modeling
Data Modeling
Data Modeling
text:
Many-to-Many Relationship
A many-to-many relationship means many records in Entity A can connect to many records in Entity B.
Example:

Many students can enroll in many courses
Many products can appear in many orders


Explain that many-to-many relationships cannot usually be implemented directly as two tables in a relational database. They need an associative table.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Activity: Draw Cardinality
For each statement, decide the cardinality:

A department has many instructors.
A student has one university ID card.
A student enrolls in many courses, and a course has many students.
A customer places many orders.

Then sketch a simple ER diagram for each.

Give students 10 minutes. Encourage them to label relationships clearly. Afterward, review each statement and ask students how they knew the cardinality.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Resolving Many-to-Many Relationships
Many-to-many relationships are usually resolved with a bridge table, also called an associative table.





flowchart LR
  S[Student] --> E[Enrollment]
  E --> C[Course]

  classDef blue fill:#0072B2,color:#FFFFFF,stroke:#111111,stroke-width:2px
  classDef orange fill:#E69F00,color:#000000,stroke:#111111,stroke-width:2px
  classDef green fill:#009E73,color:#000000,stroke:#111111,stroke-width:2px

  class S blue
  class E orange
  class C green







Explain that Enrollment stores the connection between a student and a course. It can also store relationship-specific attributes such as enrollment date or grade.

title: Data Modeling
Data Modeling
text:
Keys in Relational Databases
Keys help identify records and connect tables.
Important key types:

Primary key
Foreign key
Composite key
Candidate key


Transition from diagrams to implementation. Explain that keys are what make relationships enforceable in a relational database.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Primary Keys
A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table.
A good primary key should be:

Unique
Not missing
Stable over time
Simple to reference


Explain that primary keys prevent ambiguity. Mention that IDs are often used because names and emails can change or repeat.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Primary Key Example



student_id
first_name
last_name
email




101
Ana
Rivera
ana@example.edu


102
Jamal
Lee
jamal@example.edu


103
Mei
Chen
mei@example.edu



student_id is the primary key because it uniquely identifies each student.

Ask students why first name or last name alone would not work as a primary key. Then ask whether email is always a safe choice.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Foreign Keys
A foreign key is a field in one table that refers to the primary key in another table.
Foreign keys are used to:

Connect related tables
Enforce valid relationships
Prevent orphan records


Use the phrase parent table and child table if helpful. Explain that a foreign key makes sure a course references a real department or an enrollment references a real student.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Primary and Foreign Keys Together





flowchart LR
  D[Department table\ndepartment_id is primary key] --> C[Course table\ndepartment_id is foreign key]

  classDef blue fill:#0072B2,color:#FFFFFF,stroke:#111111,stroke-width:2px
  classDef orange fill:#E69F00,color:#000000,stroke:#111111,stroke-width:2px

  class D blue
  class C orange







Point out that the same value can be a primary key in one table and a foreign key in another. The role depends on the table where the column appears.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Activity: Find the Keys
Given these tables, identify the primary keys and foreign keys.
Student(student_id, first_name, last_name)
Course(course_id, course_name, department_id)
Enrollment(enrollment_id, student_id, course_id, enrolled_on)
Questions:

Which fields uniquely identify rows?
Which fields connect tables?
Which table resolves a many-to-many relationship?


Give students 8 minutes. Ask them to mark primary keys with PK and foreign keys with FK. Review that Enrollment connects Student and Course.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Composite Keys
A composite key uses two or more columns together to uniquely identify a row.
Example:
Enrollment(student_id, course_id, term)
Together, these fields can identify one student’s enrollment in one course during one term.

Explain that composite keys are useful when no single field is enough. Also mention that some designers still add a separate enrollment_id for convenience.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Why Normalization?
Normalization organizes data to reduce:

Repetition
Update problems
Insert problems
Delete problems
Confusing dependencies


Transition to data quality. Explain that normalization helps prevent the same fact from being stored in multiple places.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Unnormalized Data Example











student_id
student_name
course_1
course_2
instructor_1
instructor_2




101
Ana Rivera
Database Systems
Statistics
Dr. Kim
Dr. Patel


102
Jamal Lee
Database Systems
Programming
Dr. Kim
Dr. Gomez



Problems:

Repeating course columns
Hard to add a third course
Instructor data is mixed with student data


Ask students what happens if a student takes four courses. Then ask what happens if Dr. Kim’s name changes. This motivates normalization.

title: Data Modeling
text:
26. First Normal Form
A table is in first normal form when:

Each cell stores a single value
There are no repeating groups
Each row can be uniquely identified






flowchart LR
  A[Repeating course columns] --> B[One course per row]
  B --> C[Student table plus enrollment table]

  classDef red fill:#D55E00,color:#FFFFFF,stroke:#111111,stroke-width:2px
  classDef yellow fill:#F0E442,color:#000000,stroke:#111111,stroke-width:2px
  classDef green fill:#009E73,color:#000000,stroke:#111111,stroke-width:2px

  class A red
  class B yellow
  class C green







Explain that 1NF removes repeated columns and multi-value cells. The goal is to make data row-based rather than column-repeated.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Second Normal Form
A table is in second normal form when:

It is already in first normal form
Every non-key attribute depends on the entire primary key

This mainly matters when a table has a composite key.

Define partial dependency in plain language. If a field depends on only part of a composite key, it probably belongs in another table.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Third Normal Form
A table is in third normal form when:

It is already in second normal form
Non-key fields do not depend on other non-key fields

Example problem:
student_id, student_name, department_id, department_name
department_name depends on department_id, not directly on student_id.

Explain transitive dependency as an indirect dependency. If department name depends on department ID, store department information in a Department table.
